summary:
**What the change does.** A single file, `src/View/Shortcodes/EmbedShortcodeProvider.php`. The "simple iframe" fast path in `sandboxHtml()` previously returned the third-party embed HTML verbatim (`return $html;`). The MR replaces that with a call to a new private helper `removeDangerousAttributes()`, which is meant to strip every iframe attribute outside a 13-name allowlist and to reject `javascript:`/`data:`/`vbscript:`/`file:` values in `src`. It is a hardening change, implemented entirely with regular expressions.

**What I examined.** I read the whole file (496 lines) rather than the hunk, tracing the data path end to end: `handle_shortcode()` -> `embeddableToHtml()` -> `videoEmbed()` -> `sandboxHtml()` -> `removeDangerousAttributes()`, and confirmed the sink is the unescaped `DBField::create_field('HTMLFragment', $content)` at line 228. I confirmed the source is `$extractor->code->html` (line 176), i.e. HTML returned by the remote oEmbed provider for the URL supplied in the shortcode, so it is attacker-influenced by anyone who can author an `[embed]` shortcode. I searched the repository for other callers or config of `sandboxHtml`, `removeDangerousAttributes`, `domains_excluded_from_sandboxing` and `sandboxed_iframe_attributes`; there are none beyond this file.

I then worked through the two new regexes character by character against the HTML5 tokenizer states:
- The outer tag regex `#^<iframe(?:"[^"]*"|'[^']*'|[^>])*>#i` — I checked that its match always covers at least as much as the browser's opening tag (its quoted alternatives are a superset of the browser's quoted-value handling), so it does not truncate the sanitised region. I also tried to construct catastrophic backtracking against it; because `sandboxHtml` has already guaranteed a `>` exists, every path I tried terminates quickly, so I did not report ReDoS.
- The `src` scheme check — entity decoding (`ENT_QUOTES|ENT_HTML5`) plus stripping of `\x00-\x20` defeats the usual `jav	ascript:` and `:` obfuscations, and `strtolower` on the parsed scheme handles case. I could not construct a working bypass of that check on its own.
- The inner attribute regex — this is where the control fails, and it is the finding I reported.

**Conclusion.** One finding: the inner regex on line 446 requires `[\s/]+` before an attribute name, but the HTML5 "after attribute value (quoted)" state starts a new attribute on *any* non-whitespace character. `<iframe src="x"onload="alert(1)">` therefore passes through `removeDangerousAttributes()` completely untouched and is emitted as an `HTMLFragment`. The same gap also bypasses the `src` scheme check. The added function does not provide the containment it implements.

Note on attribution: because the pre-change code returned `$html` raw on this same path, this is an incomplete new control rather than a newly introduced weakness — the exploit worked before the MR too. I reported it because the MR is what claims to close it, and merging it as-is records the path as fixed when it is not.

One secondary observation I deliberately did **not** report as a finding, since I could not tie it to a concrete exploit: the allowlist omits `sandbox`, so an iframe that a provider deliberately shipped with `sandbox="..."` will have that restriction stripped by the new code. That is a small theoretical loss of defence rather than a traced weakness.
unresolved: Whether an unauthenticated path can reach `handle_shortcode` with an attacker-chosen URL. I set `reachable_without_authentication: no` on the basis that inserting an `[embed]` shortcode requires content-authoring rights, but the shortcode parser's callers live outside this file and I did not find them in this repository — if any front-end form or API renders user-supplied shortcode content, the finding is unauthenticated.

The precise trust level of the `Embeddable`/`EmbedContainer` implementation. I confirmed the HTML originates from `$extractor->code->html` but the extractor itself is injected (`Injector::inst()->create(Embeddable::class, ...)`) and its implementation is not in the changed set; I assumed it performs no HTML sanitisation of its own, which is consistent with the existence of `sandboxHtml`.
No test file for `EmbedShortcodeProvider` exists in this repository snapshot, so I could not check the author's own intended bypass cases against the new sanitizer.

I could not definitively rule out catastrophic backtracking in the outer regex `#^<iframe(?:"[^"]*"|'[^']*'|[^>])*>#i`. The alternation is ambiguous (a quoted run can also be consumed character-by-character via `[^>]`), which is the classic precondition, but every failing input I constructed was rescued quickly by a reachable `>`. If it can be made to fail, `preg_replace_callback` returns null against a `: string` return type, which would be a TypeError rather than a hang.

The `domains_excluded_from_sandboxing` suffix match at line 490 uses `str_ends_with($domain, $excludedDomain)`, which matches `evil-youtube.com` against a configured `youtube.com`. This is pre-existing and unchanged by the MR, and the default config is empty, so I did not trace it to an exploit — but it is a real suffix-matching weakness for any site that populates that config.

verdict.reason: 1 finding(s) reported, none at or above the high threshold.

findings.title: Iframe attribute sanitizer misses attributes not preceded by whitespace (XSS)
findings.severity_derivation: state_change → high; authentication required → medium; needs a victim to act → low
findings.description:
`sandboxHtml()` now routes the "simple iframe" fast path through the newly added `removeDangerousAttributes()` (line 392), which is intended to strip everything outside an allowlist (so event handlers such as `onload` are removed) before the provider-supplied HTML is emitted unescaped via `DBField::create_field('HTMLFragment', $content)` in `videoEmbed()` (line 228).

The inner attribute regex on line 446 only recognises an attribute when it is preceded by one or more `[\s/]` characters. The HTML5 tokenizer does not require that: in the "after attribute value (quoted)" state, any character that is not whitespace, `/` or `>` is a `missing-whitespace-between-attributes` parse error and is *reconsumed in the before-attribute-name state*, i.e. it starts a new attribute. So `<iframe src="x"onload="alert(1)">` is parsed by every browser as an iframe with an `onload` handler, while the regex, after consuming the ` src="x"` match, resumes scanning at `onload="alert(1)">`, finds no leading whitespace or slash anywhere, and therefore never matches — the handler is copied through verbatim by `preg_replace_callback`.

The gate above it does not stop this either: `preg_match('#^<iframe[^>]*>#', $html)`, `preg_match('#</iframe\s*>$#', $html)` and `substr_count($html, '<') <= 2` are all satisfied by a single iframe element whose payload contains no `<`.

The same gap defeats the `src` scheme check on lines 454-460: `<iframe title="a"src="javascript:alert(1)">` never produces a match for the second attribute, so the `javascript:` value is never inspected.

Net effect: the added function does not deliver the containment it implements, and the "simple iframe" branch still emits attacker-controlled event handlers into the page instead of the `data:` sandboxed iframe that the `else` branch (lines 396-414) would have produced.
findings.exploit_scenario:
A CMS author with only content-editing rights (the privilege level the sandboxing feature exists to contain) inserts `[embed url="https://attacker.example/page"]` into page content. The attacker's server responds with oEmbed/OpenGraph metadata of type `video` whose embed code is:

`<iframe src="https://attacker.example/v"onload="fetch('/admin/security/add',{...})"></iframe>`

`handle_shortcode()` -> `embeddableToHtml()` -> `videoEmbed()` -> `sandboxHtml()` sees a well-formed single iframe with only two `<` characters, so it takes the fast path and calls `removeDangerousAttributes()`. That function strips nothing, because `onload` is not preceded by whitespace. The HTML is cached and rendered unescaped as an `HTMLFragment`. Any visitor — including an administrator previewing or browsing the page — executes the attacker's JavaScript in the site's origin, allowing session-riding requests such as privilege escalation or content modification as that user.
findings.recommendation: Do not sanitise HTML with regular expressions here; the tokenizer rules the browser applies cannot be reproduced this way. Parse the fragment with `DOMDocument`/`masterminds/html5` (or SilverStripe's `HTMLValue`), iterate the element's real attribute nodes, drop any name not in `$allowed`, validate `src` against an http/https allowlist, and re-serialise via `HTML::createTag('iframe', $attrs)` so the output is built from known-good attributes rather than edited in place. If a regex approach must be kept as an interim measure, at minimum treat any character following a quoted attribute value as an attribute-name boundary (i.e. make the separator `(?:[\s/]+|(?<=["\']))`) and fail closed — fall through to the `data:` sandboxed-iframe branch — whenever the opening tag contains anything the parser does not fully account for.
